projects.name: 3.2.19.1 - Strengthening Evidence Based Decision Making for Citizen Security in the Caribbean (CariSecure)
projects.description:
CariSECURE will improve the decision-making process in Caribbean public institutions by providing quantitative and qualitative tools for analysis and supporting their incorporation into national citizen security policies and actions. The Project aims to transform quantitative data into useful qualitative information, enabling public servants to make data-informed decisions and to use this information to develop policies and programmes that address key crime and violence problems identified in the data.

Towards achieving this, the CariSECURE project will rely on the intervention logic used by Centers for Disease Control (CDC) Public Health Approach to Violence Prevention which focuses on preventing disease or injury from occurring rather than treating consequences. In particular, the project will focus on (i) processing data required to define the problem; (ii) transforming it into information to identify risk and protective factors of youth involvement in crime and violence; and (iii) facilitating decision making required to develop preventive policies and programmes.

It is therefore expected, that by improving the availability, comparability, reliability and analysis of disaggregated citizen security data, the Project will complement the on-going efforts for improving the quality of preventive policy decisions made in target institutions, and thus contribute to the overall reduction of youth crime and violence in the framework the USAID Youth Empowerment Services (YES) project.

projects.name: 4.1.4.1 - Climate Change Adaptation in the Eastern Caribbean Fisheries Sector
projects.description:
In addition to the threats of climate change, the fisheries sector is already suffering from other pressures such as: overfishing, loss of habitat, pollution, disturbance of coral reefs, and invasive species, with climate change further exacerbating these problems. While the project cannot alter the projections for climate change in the region, it can address the barriers to adaptation in order to increase resilience and reduce vulnerability to climate change impacts. 
The barriers this project will address:
Barrier 1: Insufficient understanding and awareness of climate change vulnerability of the fisheries sector at the regional, national and local level
Barrier 2: Limited fisherfolk, aquaculturists and coastal community resilience to climate change and variability 
Barrier 3: Ineffective mainstreaming of climate change adaptation in fisheries at multi-level fisheries governance 

The Project’s Objective is to increase resilience and reduce vulnerability to climate change impacts in the Eastern Caribbean fisheries sector, through introduction of adaptation measures in fisheries management and capacity building of fisherfolk and aquaculturists.
projects.outcome: Output 4.1.4 - Resiliency to climate change for fisherfolk, aquaculturists and coastal communities strengthened

projects.name: 1.1.8.5 - Decent Work Country Programme (DWCP) for Suriname
projects.description:
Decent Work Country Programmes (DWCPs) have been established as the main vehicle for delivery of ILO support to countries. DWCPs have two basic objectives. They promote decent work as a key component of national development strategies. At the same time they organise ILO knowledge, instruments, advocacy and cooperation at the service of tripartite constituents in a results-based framework to advance the Decent Work Agenda within the fields of comparative advantage of the Organization. 
The DWCP for Suriname will focus on 3 broad objectives: 
1. Economic diversification and social progress; 
2. Strengthening the rights and compliance agenda; and 
3. Increased tripartite capacity to advance the Decent Work Agenda and social dialogue.

To realize these objectives, the ILO will support tripartite partners in undertaking the following key interventions: 
1) Training  for Labour Inspectors and Social Workers to strengthen capacity to monitor compliance as well as Child Labour
2) Undertake research and awareness-raising activities of strenghtened employment services
3) Training to increase social dialogue and strenghten tripartite relationship between government, workers and employers
4) Support economic diversification through expanded entrepeneurship, cooperatives, value chain development and productivity improvement in the work place.
5)  Carry out surveys on the informal sector, wages, tourism employment, and baseline study on employability
6) Complete labour market information system (LMIS) at Ministry of Labour and improve capacity of triparite partners to utilise it
projects.outcome: Output 1.1.8 - National capacity is improved to achieve full and productive employment, decent work and equal pay for work of equal value for all women and men including youth and persons with disability.

projects.name: 1.2.1.9 - Safeguarding and Protecting the Most Vulnerable: Enhancing Jamaica's Shock Responsive Social Protection Mechanisms in support of vulnerable Groups
projects.description:
This is part of MPTF Window 2: Reduce Social Impact and Promote Economic Response: This response strategy will seek to build on and expand the investments which have been made over the past years in supporting national systems, drawing on lessons learned to protect, plan and prioritize the needs of the most vulnerable populations targeted under the Government of Jamaica’s National Social Protection Policy and Strategy. The solutions will support socio-economic needs and will focus mainly on shock responsive social protection strategies - characterized by vertical (increasing transfer amounts) and horizontal (increasing the number of persons) expansion of existing social protection programmes targeting vulnerable households (families with children with disabilities, pregnant and lactating women and female headed households in rural areas). The solutions will be organized under 2 main areas targeting vulnerable groups that may
be disproportionately impacted by the economic fall-out as a result of COVID-19. The measures taken by the government to mitigate the impact of COVID-19 has affected people’s livelihoods. This project will consider social protection measures for those who, due to COVID-19, have lost their income and are unable to provide for their families; ensure that social protection services reaches the population without discrimination.

projects.name: 1.2.1.4 - Win-Win Gender Equality Means Good Business in Jamaica
projects.description:
Win-Win Gender Equality Means Good Business Programme is a joint UN Women/ILO initiative, coordinated by UN Women and funded by the European Union's Partnership Instrument. It was designed to promote the business case for gender equality through the private sector and increase women’s economic empowerment and leadership as the basis for sustainable, inclusive and equitable growth. The goal is to promote the economic empowerment of women through acknowledging the role of women as beneficiaries and partners of growth and development and increasing commitment and capacities of private and public actors to drive organizational change regarding gender equality and women´s empowerment.

The ILO (with the Support of the European Union and UN WOMEN) is supporting capacity development of the Jamaica Employers' Federation (JEF) to analyze and organize data and produce a study on Women Entrepreneurship Development (WED). Data will be sourced from business women across all sectors of the economy. The study will identify institutions to be strengthened and opportunities/services to be facilitated to support women entrepreneurs.

UN Women contribution to the programme include the following:
1. Map networks and associations of women in top leadership positions in business sector, businesswomen and national and regional corporate commercial associations, chambers and networks in Latin America and the Caribbean and European countries. 
2. Build the supply side of procurement capacities of women entrepreneurs and businesswomen to compete for procurement opportunities with companies (training and peer to peer exchange).
3. Develop methodologies, knowledge products, tools and trainings to strengthen capacities of networks and associations of women in business to increase number of women in top leadership positions; and to increase skills of women entrepreneurs. 
4. Strengthen national women’s machineries capacities to convene private sector and other partners at the national level. 
5. Outreach to gather new Women Empowerment Principles (WEPs) signatories - through high level dialogue with Jamaican private and international companies. 
6. Conduct research on the promotion of gender equality in Corporate Social Responsibility actions, corporate procurement policy (including and associated businesses), gender pay gap focused in private companies, non-discriminatory work places and sexual harassment.
7. Design and implement campaigns to advocate and raise awareness to promote gender equality in the private sector, non-discriminatory work places, sexual harassment and to address the gender pay gap.
8. Design training methodologies and tools on: gender pay gap focused on private companies, gender responsive procurement, non-discriminatory work places, and sexual harassment in the workplace.
9. Train and coach pilot enterprises to develop and implement action plans on gender equality in the private sector.
10. Refine and make available tools for companies to voluntarily report progress in the implementation of WEPs Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) and Gender Gap Analysis, for example, in partnership with on-going global initiatives.
11. Promote incentives for companies to enjoy recognition of their advances (Seals, Awards, etc.) in collaboration with the Bureau of Gender Affairs, Jamaica Stock Exchange and Chamber of Commerce.
12. Promote exchange of experiences between national and regional corporate commercial associations, chambers and networks and advocate for implementation of WEPs in LAC.
13. Expand/translate online platforms (using the existing UN Women platform www.empowerwomen.org, and EU platforms) to document and facilitate peer-to-peer learning and exchange of experiences between companies and unions in LAC and European countries; and to document good practices.
14. Collaborate with UNDP and the Mona School of Business to conduct EU/LAC bi-regional policy dialogues on the benefits of a gender responsive private sector in achieving sustainable development.

projects.name: 1.2.1.4 - Win-Win Gender Equality Means Good Business in Jamaica
projects.description:
Win-Win Gender Equality Means Good Business Programme is a joint UN Women/ILO initiative, coordinated by UN Women and funded by the European Union's Partnership Instrument. It was designed to promote the business case for gender equality through the private sector and increase women’s economic empowerment and leadership as the basis for sustainable, inclusive and equitable growth. The goal is to promote the economic empowerment of women through acknowledging the role of women as beneficiaries and partners of growth and development and increasing commitment and capacities of private and public actors to drive organizational change regarding gender equality and women´s empowerment.

The ILO (with the Support of the European Union and UN WOMEN) is supporting capacity development of the Jamaica Employers' Federation (JEF) to analyze and organize data and produce a study on Women Entrepreneurship Development (WED). Data will be sourced from business women across all sectors of the economy. The study will identify institutions to be strengthened and opportunities/services to be facilitated to support women entrepreneurs.

UN Women contribution to the programme include the following:
1. Map networks and associations of women in top leadership positions in business sector, businesswomen and national and regional corporate commercial associations, chambers and networks in Latin America and the Caribbean and European countries. 
2. Build the supply side of procurement capacities of women entrepreneurs and businesswomen to compete for procurement opportunities with companies (training and peer to peer exchange).
3. Develop methodologies, knowledge products, tools and trainings to strengthen capacities of networks and associations of women in business to increase number of women in top leadership positions; and to increase skills of women entrepreneurs. 
4. Strengthen national women’s machineries capacities to convene private sector and other partners at the national level. 
5. Outreach to gather new Women Empowerment Principles (WEPs) signatories - through high level dialogue with Jamaican private and international companies. 
6. Conduct research on the promotion of gender equality in Corporate Social Responsibility actions, corporate procurement policy (including and associated businesses), gender pay gap focused in private companies, non-discriminatory work places and sexual harassment.
7. Design and implement campaigns to advocate and raise awareness to promote gender equality in the private sector, non-discriminatory work places, sexual harassment and to address the gender pay gap.
8. Design training methodologies and tools on: gender pay gap focused on private companies, gender responsive procurement, non-discriminatory work places, and sexual harassment in the workplace.
9. Train and coach pilot enterprises to develop and implement action plans on gender equality in the private sector.
10. Refine and make available tools for companies to voluntarily report progress in the implementation of WEPs Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) and Gender Gap Analysis, for example, in partnership with on-going global initiatives.
11. Promote incentives for companies to enjoy recognition of their advances (Seals, Awards, etc.) in collaboration with the Bureau of Gender Affairs, Jamaica Stock Exchange and Chamber of Commerce.
12. Promote exchange of experiences between national and regional corporate commercial associations, chambers and networks and advocate for implementation of WEPs in LAC.
13. Expand/translate online platforms (using the existing UN Women platform www.empowerwomen.org, and EU platforms) to document and facilitate peer-to-peer learning and exchange of experiences between companies and unions in LAC and European countries; and to document good practices.
14. Collaborate with UNDP and the Mona School of Business to conduct EU/LAC bi-regional policy dialogues on the benefits of a gender responsive private sector in achieving sustainable development.

projects.name: 3.1.3.2 - Implementation of The Foundations Programme in Trinidad & Tobago and Jamaica
projects.description:
The Foundations Programme is based on the premise that violence is intentional, and that abusive behaviours are chosen methods for gaining control over persons and situations. It began in Trinidad in 2018 and Jamaica in November 2019, as a flexible 12-module programme designed for young women and men aged 13 to 24. 
The programme’s objectives are to: (a) Empower young people to understand GBV and its genesis in gender inequalities and gender-based discrimination; (b) Promote an understanding of the consequences of GBV to partner(s), children, communities and societies in general; (c) Endow young people with knowledge, skills and attitudes for addressing conflict and responding to stress and stressors that arise in relationships; (d) Establish and model an atmosphere of respect within group relations among and between young people; (e) Promote self-sufficiency among young people in taking steps towards improving their relationships and their lives; (f) Create a network of young people who will advocate for non-violent relationships.
the programme is participant-centred and invites young people to engage in ‘thinking through’ concepts such as gender, gender socialisation, gender hierarchies and constructions of masculinity, femininity, sexuality and their impact on relationships with themselves and others. It also recognises that young people have expert knowledge about the realities of the social conditions they face in their everyday lives. Potential participants for this programme are therefore seen as competent, knowing persons who are in the best position to speak about how they live and experience gender constructions.                                                                                                                                 
The Curriculum was designed for use by experienced facilitators who are trained by professional social workers, psychologists or youth workers to work with same-sex and mixed sex groups of young people in school and community settings. Community-based settings may include a variety of naturally occurring clusters such as schools, faith-based groups and other social or recreational clubs.

projects.name: 1.2.7.2 - Support the national framework and system on Occupational Safety Health (OSH) in Guyana
projects.description:
OSH in Guyana is regulated by the Occupational Safety and Health Act (No. 32 of 1997). There is an OSH Policy adopted in 1993 which was revised in 1996. A National Plan of Action on OSH was adopted in 1996. There is no OSH Programme in Guyana. 

The ILO has been supporting Guyana since 2000 in developing OSH regulations and providing training. Technical assistance was also provided to Guyana under the RBSA funded programme in the 2012-13 biennium specifically in the capacity of OSH inspection.

The Ministry of Social Protection has been requesting the technical and financial assistance of the ILO and the lLO Office in Port of Spain has provided technical and financial support in the past biennia and signed a new DWCP in which OSH activities were mainstreamed.

The strategy to achieve the outcomes has been agreed with the Ministry of Social Protection and heavily relies on national discussion and ownership. Support was provided in the following areas:

1. new and reviewing draft regulations and reaching an agreement in the final version to be submitted to the Attorney General’s Chambers
2. finalization of the Small Artisanal Placer Mine Inspection Manual for Guyana
3. support to the adoption of an OSH System approach in line with C155 and C187, which started with the review and adoption of the OSH Policy
4. an OSH campaign in the informal sector focused on workers of the construction, agricultural and service sectors.
5. review of the OSH Act through the elaboration of an Issues report
6. capacity building on OSH in the Oil and Gas sector

Activities in the current biennium will be focused on the finalization of the review of the OSH Act, elaboration of OSH Oil and Gas Regulations and the OSH Programme, promotion of the ratification of OSH conventions and capacity building.

projects.name: 2.1.1.1 - Sexual and Reproductive Health (SRH) Legislation Desk review for the English & Dutch-speaking Caribbean
projects.description:
There is a lack and/or outdated key SRH legislation across the Caribbean to move SRH policies forward. In light of this, it was decided to conduct  a desk review of the existing legislation to make it more enforceable and relevant and analyze the gaps in line with international standards and obligations.  A consultancy is being undertaken to review and document literature related to existing legislation in relation to 12 SRH issues (Minimum age of consent for sexual activity; minimum age to access to SRH services including HIV without parental consent; Contraception; Termination of pregnancy; HIV and STIs; Marriage; Protection from discrimination; Sexual abuse and violence including incest, statutory rape, sexual abuse of minors, grooming, child pornography, rape within marriage, sexual harassment, FGM, domestic violence and emotional violence; Transactional sex; Trafficking; Comprehensive sexuality education; Pregnant learner retention and re-entry laws and policy) and 7 population groups (Minors; women; persons with disabilities; sex workers; persons living with HIV and specifically women living with HIV; LGBTI populations including gay men and Trans persons; migrants)
The revision is covering all English and Dutch Speaking Caribbean countries (22 in total) and considering the international and regional standards and obligations in regards to SRH laws as well as national legislation.

projects.name: 1.2.8.2 - Training of labour inspectors and social workers to conduct inspections for child labour in Hinterland regions (Guyana)
projects.description:
Guyana has ratified the fundamental legal instruments on child labour (United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child), ILO Worst Forms of Child Labour Convention, 1999 (No. 182) and the ILO Minimum Age Convention, 1973 (No. 138) and is a signatory to the Regional Initiative Latin America and the Caribbean Free of Child Labour (RI). Despite this commitment, child work in Guyana exists across sexes, age groups, ethnic origins and areas of settlement.
As reflected in the Guyana DWCP 2017-2021 (which was formalised in December 2017), the issue of Child Labour is a key area for attention under the first of 3 core Country Programme Priorities.
During 2018-2019, the Government with support from UNICEF, developed and formalized a National Policy Toward the Elimination of Child Labour, and subsequently developed a National Action Plan on Child Labour based on the policy. The NAP was validated in consultations with key stakeholders and is pending final Ministerial endorsement prior to implementation.  In this period ILO provide technical assistance for capacity building which yielded country specific training materials on child labour inspections and execution of government-led, national training workshop for the labour inspectorate and key officials in other Ministries and agencies.
In 2019, the Government of Guyana also submitted an official request to the ILO Regional Director indicating interest in participation in the ongoing pilot of the ILO-ECLAC Child Labour Risk Identification model (CLRISK). This innovative tool was developed by the Regional Initiative Latin American and the Caribbean (RI) to equip member States to analyse existing national statistics and records to arrive at reliable predictions of local level, geographic spread of risk/ vulnerability factors which predispose children and teens to early entry into work or exposure to worst forms of child labour (WFCL). The results of the model would inform policy-making and targeted, multi-sectoral interventions allowing for more effective and efficient use of national resources to combat CL. The application of the CLRISK was further inscribed in the DWCP Implementation plan established by the national DWCP implementation oversight committee. Initial sensitization and planning meetings on the model with stakeholders were held in 2019.
For the biennium the following programme of work is proposed to support completion of the CL Risk Model and capacity building for enforcement and implementation of child labour strategies:
v Application of the ILO- ECLAC CL Risk model- within framework of the RI and MAP ’16 Project
- Engagements with Ministries, national agencies and other International development partners (UNICEF, IOM etc.) to identify and obtain access to relevant sources of data and administrative records
- Training of national officials in application of the statistical model (
- Engagements with national stakeholders to determine/ validate key indicators and preliminary results
- Technical expertise (EXCOLL) to develop maps and territorial characterizations (risk or vulnerability profiles)
- Finalization and launch of final CL Risk Maps/ Profiles for Guyana

v Technical support for National coordination and implementation of the National CL Action Plan (NAP)
- ILO technical support (face to face/ virtual) for inter-ministerial/ inter-institutional consultations for sensitization and roll-out of the NAP
v General technical support on thematic issues relevant to CL/ WFCL

projects.name: 1.2.7.3 - Develop a programme to improve productivity in small and medium-sized enterprises and cooperatives in Guyana
projects.description:
Within the context of Guyana’s Decent Work Country Programme (2017-2021), ILO constituents agreed to develop a national framework or policies for the creation of an environment conducive to sustainable enterprises. Under this outcome, the Government of Guyana committed among its priorities to push for further diversification and improvement in the output of value added products in sectors with opportunity for export growth. The constituents also listed the need to update the regulatory framework for cooperatives to ensure they regain a key position in the green economy and the export-oriented business environment.
In 2019, the ILO and the Cooperatives Department of the Ministry of Social Protection worked on a dual process of gathering international good practices in cooperative legislation and gathering the insights into the limitations of the current legislation as experienced by cooperatives themselves. While the first part was completed and the Cooperatives Office has an initial compilation of items to be reviewed in the current legislation in light of international good practice, the regional consultations were postponed partly due to limited human resources of the Cooperatives Office. These consultations remain however an important input into the updating of the legislation and getting the buy-in from those who will be ultimately impacted. 
In 2017, the ILO and the Ministry of Business commissioned a rapid market assessment to identify agricultural value chains with growth and export potential. The study identified mango and peppers as two potential value chains. In discussions around the study with stakeholders, the need for better information flows, including the periodic gathering, recording, safekeeping and use of data, was listed as a key impediment to products successfully making it to national and international markets in the quality and quantity needed. Stakeholders expressed the need for a platform that would support better information flows, particularly linked to what the needs and requirements are from the market so that stakeholders and supporting organizations can best work with actors along the value chain to respond to the market demands.
Within the 2020/2021 biennium and in line with the DWCP’s Priority 2 on sustainable livelihoods through improving economic opportunities, the ILO seeks to strengthen the Cooperative Department’s outreach and capacity to gather insights from its members on opportunities and limitations of the current Cooperative Societies’ Act, as well as to prepare Cooperatives to better assess, prepare and manage risks (especially those related to natural disasters and climate change)
In addition, ILO through a self-funded project (RBSA) entitled Caribbean Resilience and developed with a view to support the country’s current development plan (Green State Development Strategy 2040), will seek to strengthen constituents ability to support enterprises (including cooperatives) in planning, managing and responding to natural disasters and either greening or emerging in green sectors. To do so, a special focus on resilience, risk management and prevention will be included as a cross-cutting theme in both consultations with cooperatives and designing a platform for information flows with specific agro processing value chains. ILO will also seek to sensitize ILO constituents and broader enterprise development actors to the positive links between increasing resilience, transitioning to green sectors and greener practices, improving productivity and strengthening working conditions within the context of the Green State Development Strategy 2040 (GSDS 2040) of Guyana. The objective will be to help constituents continue to work for further diversification of the economy and avoid over concentrating on the sector of oil and gas.

projects.description:
During the period 2017 - 2019 the ILO is supporting the National Training Agency of Trinidad and Tobago (NTA), to conduct research on the status of employability skills. This follows concerns of expressed by Trinidad and Tobago employers about the lack of employability skills (soft skills) of youth across the country. The purpose of the study is to gain a better understanding of skills that enhance employability, and those which are lacking within enterprises in Trinidad and Tobago. The ultimate objective is to close the skills gap in the curriculum and the Standards for Caribbean Vocational Qualification (CVQ). The data collection involves feedback of both employers and workers.
The study is guided by the Conclusions on Skills for Improved Productivity, Employment growth and Development, International Labour Conference, 2008, and ILO Recommendation 195 on Human Resources Development, Education, Training and Lifelong learning.

projects.name: 3.1.9.1 - Multi Country Boarder Security to Prevent and Fight Human Trafficking in Jamaica, Haiti and Dominica Republic.
projects.description: The project will contribute to increasing the prevention efforts and fight against trafficking in persons in Jamaica, Haiti and the Dominican Republic. This will be achieved by raising awareness and understanding of the risks of trafficking in persons for at-risk populations in target communities, especially in border areas between the Dominican Republic and Haiti and in rural areas in Jamaica. An innovative evidence-based and participatory campaign on human trafficking will be implemented in target communities in Jamaica, Haiti and the Dominican Republic with key at- risk groups. The focus will be on at-risk groups identified in communities in border areas in Haiti and the Dominican Republic and in rural areas in Jamaica as very few interventions in these countries have focused on these communities. Regarding the fight against trafficking in persons, the project will aim to strengthen the key national institutions’ capacity to investigate and prosecute offenders of the crime with a victim- centered, human rights and gender sensitive approach. This will be achieved through implementation of specialized training to targeted audiences, fostering collaboration among criminal justice system institutions. The project will also aim to develop standard operating procedures for key stakeholders to guide them in their specific roles to combat trafficking in persons. Relevant stakeholders will be trained on the SOPs to ensure adherence to these guidelines. Furthermore, bilateral and regional cooperation and mutual understanding will be fostered by holding bilateral and trilateral roundtables and workshops. In Haiti and in the Dominican Republic, activities will be focused in the land border areas.

The CARICOM Model is based on a long tested global WHO model which is considered internationally to be the best practice for national, population-based studies on GBV. The COHSOD confirmed that – with UN Women support - the Model should be modified to fit the Caribbean context, and then piloted in a number of countries, using a strategy which builds statistical capacity within CARICOM to support the eventual conducting of the survey in all CARICOM Member States. Specifically, it was agreed with COHSOD that an initial pilot would take place in a large CARICOM country (Jamaica – on going) and one small island state in the Eastern Caribbean (proposed – Grenada). UN Women has contracted the Global Women’s Institute (GWI) of George Washington University to provide technical advice and support to the implementation of the Prevalence Survey, where required.

projects.name: 4.1.26.12 - Provide emergency assistance through cash-based and in-kind transfers to shock-affected people
projects.description: Where available, WFP will build on pre-existing vulnerability data and integrated information management systems to accelerate an emergency response that is complemented by joint post-disaster assessments, including gender and age analyses, to ensure equitable benefits for all. WFP will seek to scale up and support social protection programmes by providing CBTs to an expanded number of beneficiaries through national distribution systems. Where in-kind food distributions are necessary due to a lack of functioning social protection systems or markets, WFP will distribute life-saving rations in the first phase of a response. As with CBTs, in-kind distributions will be delivered in coordination with national authorities and humanitarian actors providing complementary activities such as shelter and non-food items. Where appropriate, WFP will provide multi-purpose cash transfers to meet essential needs beyond food and nutrition. WFP’s assistance will be combined with limited social and behaviour change communication to address affected populations’ vulnerability during the emergency response. Conditional assistance may be introduced over time, in coordination with broader recovery efforts by partners, to help restore livelihoods and reduce exposure to future shocks in a gender-equitable manner.

projects.description:
Training of health care workers in support of the implementation of the “Global plan of action to strengthen the role of the health system within a national multisectoral response to address interpersonal violence, in particular against women and girls, and against children”.

This programme in based on the understanding that Violence damages women’s health in many ways, with both immediate and long-term consequences, which can be both obvious and hidden from view. Women who experience violence are more likely to seek health care though they usually do not disclose violence as the underlying reason for seeking care. Health care providers, therefore, have an important role to play in identifying women who experience violence, and responding to them with empathy. In order for health care providers to be able to respond appropriately, health systems need to be strengthened so that women receive high-quality and respectful care.

projects.name: 2.2.1.7 - Social Determinants of Health Study for NCDs
projects.description: Support the Government of Jamaica to document the relationship between the Social Determinants of Health and NCDs at a population level to inform policy and legislation. The social determinants of health (SDH) are defined by the World Health Organization as "the conditions in which people are born, grow, work, live, and age, and the wider set of forces and systems shaping the conditions of daily life". These forces and systems include economic policies and systems, development agendas, social norms and policies, and political systems. These conditions can be very different for various population subgroups, and can lead to disparities in health outcomes. The experience of such conditions may simply be unavoidably different, in which case they are considered inequalities, or they may in fact be unnecessary and avoidable, in which case they are considered inequities and therefore appropriate targets for policies designed to increase equity.
